scenes.title: Six lenses on the same experience
scenes.sub: Disorder · dissociation · addiction · attention · coping · skeptics
scenes.say: Chapter two. Six lenses on what maladaptive daydreaming fundamentally is.
First, a recall from chapter one. What separates a healthy daydream from a maladaptive one?
scenes.sayA: A healthy daydream ends in an action, like a title or a plan. A maladaptive one replaces the action and keeps looping, with immersion, compulsion and cost.
scenes.a: Healthy: ends in an action. Maladaptive: replaces it and loops.

scenes.by: Soffer-Dudek et al. 2025, MD's own proponents
scenes.text: It could arguably be categorised as a *behavioural addiction*, an *obsessive–compulsive spectrum disorder* or a unique subtype of ~ADHD~.
scenes.say: Researchers disagree about what MD fundamentally is. Even its leading proponents admit it could arguably be classed as a behavioural addiction, an obsessive compulsive spectrum disorder, or a unique type of ADHD. So let us look through six lenses.

scenes.head: Six lenses
scenes.say: The six lenses are: a distinct disorder, dissociative absorption, addiction or compulsion, an attention problem, coping and escape, and finally, the skeptics.

scenes.head: Lens 1 · A distinct disorder: what MD travels with
scenes.say: Lens one says MD is its own syndrome. A twenty twenty-five meta-analysis combined 40 studies and nearly 25,000 people. MD was linked with distress at 0.49, shame at 0.45, dissociation at 0.45, depression at 0.43, and problematic internet use at 0.40. The authors concluded it behaves like other recognised disorders.

scenes.head: In 39 people diagnosed by interview
scenes.say: Among 39 people diagnosed by interview, three in four met criteria for more than three other conditions: ADHD in 77 percent, anxiety in 72, depression in 67, and OCD-related disorders in 54.

items: No lab markers or family studies

scenes.say: The support: interviewers agree reliably, MD is stable over a year, and it responds to targeted treatment while generic approaches fail. The critique: even proponents call the criteria still somewhat arbitrary, there are no lab markers or family studies, and most samples are online volunteers. Their reply is that this objection applies to most diagnoses. Major depression reached interviewer agreement of only 0.28 in its own field trials.

scenes.head: Lens 2 · Dissociative absorption

items: Detachment rises on high-MD days, and the day after
Dissociation happens to you; MD is sought out
The fantasy is enjoyed and set up on purpose

scenes.say: Lens two is the one behind the official proposal. It says MD is a disorder of absorption and detachment. Dissociation is MD's strongest specific link, at 0.45, and feeling detached rises on high-MD days and the day after, but not the day before. It is also the basis of the official proposal. The critique: classic dissociation happens to people, while MD is sought out, enjoyed, and set up on purpose with music, solitude and movement. And much of the data comes from dissociation clinics, where MD would be over-represented anyway.

scenes.head: Lens 3 · Addiction or compulsion
items: More obsessive-compulsive symptoms the next day
scenes.say: Lens three explains the craving and the relapses. A quarter of one sample spontaneously called MD an addiction. In 14-day diaries kept by 77 people with MD, obsessive compulsive symptoms were the only thing that reliably came before a high-MD day. And more MD, in turn, predicted more of those symptoms the next day. The authors called it a vicious cycle.

scenes.text: But there is *no clear tolerance*, and unlike intrusive obsessions, the fantasy is ~satisfying~ in the short term.
scenes.note: So why does removing music matter so much? It's the cue.
scenes.say: The dissociation camp pushes back on two points. There is no clear tolerance, meaning people do not need more and more to get the same effect. And unlike intrusive obsessions, indulging a daydream storyline is satisfying in the short term. Still, the addiction lens explains the one more scene relapse, and why removing the cue, music, matters so much.

scenes.head: Lens 4 · Attention: an overlap that runs one way
items: People with MD who have ADHD
Adults with ADHD who have MD
scenes.say: Lens four matters most for your work. 77 percent of people with MD also met criteria for ADHD, but only 20 percent of adults with ADHD have MD. The overlap runs mostly one way.

scenes.by: People with both, Theodor-Katz et al. 2022
scenes.text: They viewed the attentional problem as a *resulting or secondary* factor.
scenes.note: Stimulants did next to nothing for the daydreaming
scenes.say: People with both said their attention problem was a result of the daydreaming, and researchers propose that immersive daydreaming causes inattention. In a survey of 202 sufferers, stimulant medication had next to no positive effect on the daydreaming, and some said it made it worse. So an ADHD label on its own would probably miss the target. But no study has followed both over time, so which drives which is still open.

scenes.head: Lens 5 · Coping and escape
scenes.say: Lens five explains why it started, and what it does for you. Somer described the fantasy's job as escaping stress and pain through mood enhancement and wish fulfilment, and as giving companionship and soothing. A twenty twenty-five review of 89 studies calls MD a dysfunctional coping mechanism. The mood is repaired for now, but the 13-month data show MD predicts more distress later.

scenes.text: Trauma is *not required*. The pooled link with trauma is small, about r = .20, and many people with MD had no difficult childhood.
scenes.note: When trauma is present, it shapes the plots
scenes.say: Importantly, trauma is not required. The pooled link between MD and trauma is small, about 0.2, and MD appears in many people without difficult childhoods. When trauma is present, it shapes the content. Emotional neglect goes with idealised-family plots, for example.

scenes.head: Lens 6 · The skeptics
scenes.text: If she daydreams because she's bored, maybe the things she's doing *bore her*.
scenes.note: No peer-reviewed paper argues MD isn't real
scenes.say: Lens six, the skeptics, target the label, not the suffering. Psychologist Jonathan Raskin warns against confusing difference with dysfunction, and asks pointedly: if she daydreams because she's bored, maybe the things she's doing bore her. Others say adding MD to the manuals now would be premature, given the heavy reliance on Reddit samples. But no peer-reviewed paper argues MD isn't real.

scenes.head: Each lens explains a different part of you
items: Addiction: the craving, the ‘one more scene’ relapse, why removing music matters
Coping: why uncomfortable work is the trigger, and what the fantasy gives you
Dissociation: the absorbed, detached feeling and the foggy aftermath
Attention: the cost to your focus, and why stimulants alone may miss
Skeptics: what need is the fantasy meeting that real life is not?
scenes.say: Read these lenses as views of one experience, not rival theories. The addiction lens explains the craving and the one more scene relapse, and why removing music matters. The coping lens explains why uncomfortable work is the trigger, and what the fantasy does for you in that moment. The dissociation lens explains the absorbed, detached feeling and the foggy aftermath. The attention lens explains the cost to your focus. And the skeptics leave you a useful question: if a task reliably sends you into fantasy, what need is the fantasy meeting that real life is not?
Which lens best explains why uncomfortable work, specifically, is your trigger?
scenes.sayA: The coping and escape lens. The fantasy repairs your mood in that moment, which is exactly why it returns whenever work gets hard.
scenes.a: Coping and escape: it repairs your mood in that moment

scenes.say: True or false: most adults with ADHD also have MD.
scenes.sayA: False. Most people with MD have ADHD symptoms, but only about 20 percent of adults with ADHD have MD. The overlap runs one way.
scenes.a: False. 77% of MD has ADHD; only about 20% of ADHD has MD.
